entries.meaning: To show by evidence or argument that a claim, theory, or story is false.
examples: One clean experiment can disprove a decade of theory.
The lab disproved the original finding in under a month.
Nobody has disproved her central claim yet.
By 1960 the idea had been disproven several times over.
A disproven hypothesis still teaches you something.
You can't disprove a negative, so the burden stays with the accuser.
He disproves every rumor about the company by simply showing up.

senses.head: Show something to be false
body: The core sense, and nearly the only one. The object is a claim, theory, rumor, or alibi — you disprove a statement, not a person. The -n participle disproven is standard in front of a noun (a disproven theory), but the perfect tense in edited American prose is usually has disproved. (опровергать, доказывать ложность)
examples: One clean experiment can disprove a decade of theory.
The lab disproved the original finding in under a month.
Nobody has disproved her central claim yet.
By 1960 the idea had been disproven several times over.
A disproven hypothesis still teaches you something.

senses.head: disprove a negative — the argument phrase
body: A fixed idiom about the burden of proof: you can't disprove a negative means the person making the claim has to support it, not the skeptic. Common in debate, law, and science writing. (доказать отсутствие (чего-л.), опровергнуть отрицательное утверждение)
examples: You can't disprove a negative, so the burden stays with the accuser.
He disproves every rumor about the company by simply showing up.

entries.forms: disprove /dɪsˈpruv/ · disproved /dɪsˈpruvd/ · disproven /dɪsˈpruvən/ · American prose more often uses disproved
entries.register: everyday — ordinary in argument, news, and science writing; nothing marked about it
entries.contrast: Prefix plus prove, and it behaves exactly like its base verb. Both participles are correct, but edited American writing uses has disproved noticeably more than has disproven, while the -n form is most at home in front of a noun: a disproven theory. The past tense is always disproved: ✗ he disproven it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic verb of demonstration, comfortable in the progressive (they're disproving it point by point). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is a claim, theory, rumor, or alibi, and it is obligatory: disprove her central claim; ✗ the lab disproved is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes — nobody has disproved her central claim yet, by 1960 the idea had been disproven several times over.

entries.meaning: To cut letters or a design into a hard surface — and, figuratively, to fix something permanently in the mind.
examples: They engrave the winner's name on the cup every June.
The jeweler engraved our initials inside the ring.
She has engraved glass for thirty years.
He engraves by hand, without a machine.
Winslow Homer engraved wood blocks for the illustrated weeklies.
US currency is still engraved rather than photographed onto the plate.
The bank note had been engraved by hand in 1890.
That afternoon is engraved on my memory.
Thirty years of practice have engraved the movement into her hands.
The rule had been engraved in every trainee's head by week two.
Nineteenth-century hymns speak of a name engraven on the heart.

senses.head: Cut letters or a design into a surface
body: The everyday sense, used of metal, glass, stone, and jewelry. In modern American English the verb is simply regular: engraved serves as both past and participle, and ✗ has engraven is a nineteenth-century form nobody writes now. (гравировать, вырезать (надпись))
examples: They engrave the winner's name on the cup every June.
The jeweler engraved our initials inside the ring.
She has engraved glass for thirty years.
He engraves by hand, without a machine.

senses.head: Make a printing plate; produce an engraving
body: The printmaking and currency sense: cutting an image into a plate or block so it can be inked and printed. Mostly technical or historical now. (гравировать (печатную форму), делать гравюру)
examples: Winslow Homer engraved wood blocks for the illustrated weeklies.
US currency is still engraved rather than photographed onto the plate.
The bank note had been engraved by hand in 1890.

senses.head: Fix permanently in the memory
body: Figurative, usually passive and followed by on or in: engraved on my memory. The nineteenth-century form engraven survives only as an echo of graven image in older hymns and poetry. (запечатлеть, врезать (в память))
examples: That afternoon is engraved on my memory.
Thirty years of practice have engraved the movement into her hands.
The rule had been engraved in every trainee's head by week two.
Nineteenth-century hymns speak of a name engraven on the heart.

entries.forms: engrave /ɪnˈɡreɪv/ · engraved /ɪnˈɡreɪvd/ · engraven /ɪnˈɡreɪvən/ · the American participle is engraved
entries.register: everyday — the ordinary American word for what a jeweler or a trophy shop does
entries.contrast: In modern American English engrave is simply a regular verb: engraved is both the past and the participle. Engraven is a nineteenth-century form you will meet only in older books and as an echo of graven image — never write ✗ has engraven. Same story as grave, the older verb this one was built from.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: cutting a surface, making a printing plate, and fixing something in the memory.
entries.transitivity: both — normally transitive (engraved our initials inside the ring), but the object drops when the technique is the point: he engraves by hand.
entries.passive: yes, and the memory sense is nearly always passive — that afternoon is engraved on my memory; also US currency is still engraved rather than photographed onto the plate.

entries.meaning: To bite at something over and over with small, wearing bites — literally, or in the sense of a worry that keeps working away at you.
examples: Puppies gnaw on anything within reach.
Something gnawed a hole in the bottom of the bag.
Mice have gnawed through the insulation again.
The dog gnaws the same bone every evening.
Doubt had gnawed at him all week.
The question gnaws at me every time I drive past that exit.
Guilt gnawed at her for years afterward.
The river gnaws a little more of the bank away each spring.
Rust has gnawed the bottom of both doors.
In older writing you will find a rope described as gnawn clear through.

senses.head: Bite at something repeatedly
body: The literal sense, typical of rodents, dogs, and teething children. Often with on or at when no hole is made, and with a direct object when one is. The g is silent in every form, /nɔ/. (грызть, глодать)
examples: Puppies gnaw on anything within reach.
Something gnawed a hole in the bottom of the bag.
Mice have gnawed through the insulation again.
The dog gnaws the same bone every evening.

senses.head: gnaw at — nag, torment
body: Figurative, with a worry, doubt, guilt, or unanswered question as the subject. Almost always with at, and the feeling is persistent rather than sharp. (грызть, мучить, не давать покоя (о сомнении, тревоге))
examples: Doubt had gnawed at him all week.
The question gnaws at me every time I drive past that exit.
Guilt gnawed at her for years afterward.

senses.head: Wear away gradually
body: Of water, wind, rust, or inflation eating slowly into something. Written rather than spoken register; gnawn is rare enough in American print that you should write has gnawed. (подтачивать, разъедать, размывать)
examples: The river gnaws a little more of the bank away each spring.
Rust has gnawed the bottom of both doors.
In older writing you will find a rope described as gnawn clear through.

entries.forms: gnaw /nɔ/ · gnawed /nɔd/ · gnawn /nɔn/ · the American participle is gnawed
entries.register: everyday — common of animals literally and of worry figuratively
entries.contrast: The g is silent in every form — /nɔ/, not ✗ /ɡnɔ/. Gnawn is rare enough that most Americans have never seen it in print; write has gnawed. Compare saw and whipsaw, which share the same /ɔ/ vowel and the same optional, mostly British -n participle.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and iterative (repeated small bites); the figurative gnaw at is just as dynamic, not stative.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when a hole results (something gnawed a hole in the bag), intransitive with on or at when none does (puppies gnaw on anything, doubt gnawed at him).
entries.passive: restricted — fine with a real direct object: the insulation has been gnawed through again. The gnaw at pattern resists it: ✗ he was gnawed at by doubt.

entries.meaning: An old verb meaning to carve or cut into a hard surface, now alive almost only in its participle graven.
examples: Older writers use grave where we would now say engrave.
The mason graved the family name across the lintel.
Those letters had been graved into the stone centuries earlier.
The printmaker graves the plate first and pulls a proof afterward.
The commandment against graven images is the second one.
Two hard years have graven deep lines in his face.
The motto was graven over the doorway in Latin.

senses.head: Carve or cut into stone or metal
body: Archaic. Not the noun grave ("burial place") or the adjective grave ("serious") — this is the old verb that engrave replaced. For anything you write yourself, use engrave or carve. (гравировать, высекать, вырезать)
examples: Older writers use grave where we would now say engrave.
The mason graved the family name across the lintel.
Those letters had been graved into the stone centuries earlier.
The printmaker graves the plate first and pulls a proof afterward.

senses.head: graven — carved; cut deep
body: The participle is the only part of the verb still in circulation, and it works as an adjective: the graven image of the Ten Commandments, or lines graven in a face by hard years. Slightly biblical or literary in tone. (изваянный, высеченный; врезавшийся (в память, в лицо))
examples: The commandment against graven images is the second one.
Two hard years have graven deep lines in his face.
The motto was graven over the doorway in Latin.

entries.forms: grave /ɡreɪv/ · graved /ɡreɪvd/ · graven /ˈɡreɪvən/
entries.register: archaic — the verb itself died out; only graven image keeps the participle alive
entries.contrast: Not the noun grave ("burial place") or the adjective grave ("serious") — this is an old verb meaning "carve," now almost completely replaced by engrave. Only the participle is still in circulation, and only as an adjective: the graven image of the Ten Commandments, or lines deeply graven in a face. For everyday use, write engrave or carve.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic verb of carving, but archaic; only the participle graven is still in circulation, and it works as an adjective (a graven image).
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the lettering or the surface worked: the mason graved the family name across the lintel.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is where the verb survives: the motto was graven over the doorway, those letters had been graved into the stone centuries earlier.

entries.meaning: To cut or chop something hard with heavy blows — and, in the commonest American use, to stick closely to a line, a plan, or a principle.
examples: They still hew the timbers by hand at the restoration site.
He hewed the beam square with a broadax.
Masons have hewn stone on this hillside since the 1800s.
The cabin walls were hewn from a single stand of pine.
The committee has hewed closely to the original plan.
The adaptation hewed to the novel almost line for line.
She hews to her schedule no matter who complains.
He hewed a path through the brush with a machete.
Crews have hewn a road out of solid rock.
Settlers hew a farm out of the woods one acre at a time.
Each block had been hewn to roughly the same size.
The furniture is deliberately rough-hewn.
His manner was rough-hewn but never rude.

senses.head: Chop or cut with heavy blows
body: The literal sense, used of timber and stone worked with an ax, adze, or chisel. Here the participle is hewn, especially before a noun: hewn beams, rough-hewn stone. (рубить, тесать)
examples: They still hew the timbers by hand at the restoration site.
He hewed the beam square with a broadax.
Masons have hewn stone on this hillside since the 1800s.
The cabin walls were hewn from a single stand of pine.

senses.head: hew to — stick closely to
body: Figurative and by far the commoner sense in American writing — of a policy, a script, a party line, or a schedule. This sense takes hewed in the perfect, not hewn. (твёрдо придерживаться, следовать (чему-л.))
examples: The committee has hewed closely to the original plan.
The adaptation hewed to the novel almost line for line.
She hews to her schedule no matter who complains.

senses.head: hew out — make by cutting away
body: Carving something usable out of raw material or wilderness — a path, a road, a farm, a career. Carries a flavor of hard, physical effort even when the object is abstract. (прорубать, вырубать; создавать с трудом)
examples: He hewed a path through the brush with a machete.
Crews have hewn a road out of solid rock.
Settlers hew a farm out of the woods one acre at a time.
Each block had been hewn to roughly the same size.

senses.head: rough-hewn — unpolished
body: A fixed compound adjective, used of surfaces left rough by the ax and, by extension, of a plain, unrefined manner or style. Only the participle appears in this use. (грубо отёсанный; неотёсанный, простоватый)
examples: The furniture is deliberately rough-hewn.
His manner was rough-hewn but never rude.

entries.forms: hew /hju/ · hewed /hjud/ · hewn /hjun/ · American also hewed /hjud/
entries.register: rare — a specialized woodworking verb, alive mainly in hew to and rough-hewn
entries.contrast: Both participles are alive in American English, but they divide the work. Hewn almost always stands in front of a noun — hewn beams, rough-hewn stone — while hewed carries the perfect tense: the board has hewed to the same policy for years. That second, figurative sense, hew to meaning "stick closely to," is far commoner in American writing than the woodcutting one. Note the /j/ glide, /hju/, which strew does not have.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, the literal chopping and the figurative hew to alike. Rough-hewn is a fixed adjective, not a verb form in use.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the cutting senses (hewed the beam square, hewed a path through the brush), intransitive with to in the commoner figurative sense (the committee has hewed closely to the original plan).
entries.passive: restricted — yes for the literal sense: the cabin walls were hewn from a single stand of pine, crews have hewn a road out of solid rock. No passive of hew to: ✗ the plan has been hewed to.

entries.meaning: To go from solid to liquid under heat, or to make something do that; by extension, to soften, fade out, or disappear.
examples: Melt the butter first, then whisk in the flour.
The ice melted before we got the cooler open.
All the snow has melted off the north slope.
By noon the road tar had melted into black ribbons.
The furnace holds forty tons of molten iron.
These cookies melt in your mouth.
The sugar had melted into the hot cream before she stirred it.
The cheese melted down into the bread.
Her whole face melts when the dog comes in.
He melted the second she started crying.
That video has melted every parent who has seen it.
The crowd melted away as soon as the police arrived.
His lead in the polls has melted away since June.
Whatever nerve she had melted away at the microphone.
They melted down the old trophies for the silver.
Reactor cores melt down when the coolant fails.
The toddler had melted down twice before we reached the gate.
He melted into the crowd before anyone got a photograph.
The hills melt into haze by mid-afternoon.
The suspect had melted into the neighborhood by the time the units arrived.

senses.head: Turn from solid to liquid with heat
body: The core sense, both transitive and intransitive. Melt is a regular verb today — the snow has melted, never ✗ has molten. Molten survives only as an adjective, only before a noun, and only for furnace-hot material. (плавить(ся), таять, растапливать)
examples: Melt the butter first, then whisk in the flour.
The ice melted before we got the cooler open.
All the snow has melted off the north slope.
By noon the road tar had melted into black ribbons.
The furnace holds forty tons of molten iron.

senses.head: Dissolve in the mouth or in liquid
body: Used of food that goes soft without any obvious heat, and of sugar or salt disappearing into a hot liquid. The compliment melts in your mouth is fixed. (таять (во рту), растворяться)
examples: These cookies melt in your mouth.
The sugar had melted into the hot cream before she stirred it.
The cheese melted down into the bread.

senses.head: Soften emotionally
body: Of a person, a face, or a heart giving way to affection or pity. Intransitive, informal and warm in tone; the transitive use (that melted him) is common too. (растрогаться, смягчиться, растаять)
examples: Her whole face melts when the dog comes in.
He melted the second she started crying.
That video has melted every parent who has seen it.

senses.head: melt away — disappear gradually
body: Of a crowd, a lead, a fortune, or a fear that shrinks to nothing rather than ending at once. (растаять, рассеяться, испариться)
examples: The crowd melted away as soon as the police arrived.
His lead in the polls has melted away since June.
Whatever nerve she had melted away at the microphone.

senses.head: melt down — reduce to liquid; lose control
body: Three uses of one phrasal verb: melting metal down for its material, a reactor core melting down, and — informally — a person falling apart emotionally. (переплавлять; расплавиться (об активной зоне); сорваться, устроить истерику)
examples: They melted down the old trophies for the silver.
Reactor cores melt down when the coolant fails.
The toddler had melted down twice before we reached the gate.

senses.head: melt into — blend imperceptibly
body: Of someone slipping out of sight into a crowd or a background, or of one color, sound, or landscape shading into another with no clear edge. (слиться, раствориться (в толпе, в пейзаже))
examples: He melted into the crowd before anyone got a photograph.
The hills melt into haze by mid-afternoon.
The suspect had melted into the neighborhood by the time the units arrived.

entries.forms: melt /mɛlt/ · melted /ˈmɛltɪd/ · molten /ˈmoʊltən/ · the working American participle is melted /ˈmɛltɪd/
entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Melt is a regular verb today: the snow has melted, never ✗ the snow has molten. Molten survives only as an adjective, only in front of a noun, and only for things that melt at furnace heat — molten lava, molten glass, molten steel. Nobody says ✗ molten ice cream. Compare swell, whose old -en participle is still fully in use, and rot, which stranded its -en form the same way this one did.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative: the same event stated intransitively (the ice melted) or transitively (melt the butter). Never stative, never linking; molten is an adjective only.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with the thing that changes as subject (all the snow has melted off the north slope), transitive with a causer (melt the butter first, they melted down the old trophies).
entries.passive: restricted — natural for the transitive senses: the trophies were melted down for the silver. The intransitive senses have no passive at all: ✗ the snow was melted away, ✗ the crowd was melted into.

entries.meaning: To cut down grass or standing grain — and, in mow down, to cut down people or things in numbers.
examples: I mow the yard every other Saturday all summer.
He mowed around the flower beds without being asked.
The crew has mowed the ball field twice this week.
Nothing smells better than freshly mown hay.
They mow the back forty for hay in July.
Crews mowed the alfalfa twice last season.
By the time we arrived, someone had mowed the whole hillside.
The truck jumped the curb and mowed down a row of mailboxes.
Machine guns had mowed down the first two waves.
Their closer mows down the bottom of the order every night.

senses.head: Cut grass short
body: The everyday American sense: a lawn, a field, a ball field, a ditch bank. Americans write have mowed; have mown reads as British, though mown survives here as an adjective — freshly mown grass. (косить, стричь (газон, траву))
examples: I mow the yard every other Saturday all summer.
He mowed around the flower beds without being asked.
The crew has mowed the ball field twice this week.
Nothing smells better than freshly mown hay.

senses.head: Cut a hay or grain crop
body: The older farming sense, where the point is the harvest rather than a tidy lawn. The field, not the crop, can be the object: mow the back forty. (жать, косить (сено, хлеб))
examples: They mow the back forty for hay in July.
Crews mowed the alfalfa twice last season.
By the time we arrived, someone had mowed the whole hillside.

senses.head: mow down — cut down in numbers
body: Of gunfire, a vehicle, or a disease killing or knocking down many at once, and in sports of a pitcher or team dispatching opponents easily. The idiom is always mowed down, never ✗ mown down. (скосить, смести (очередью, машиной); разгромить)
examples: The truck jumped the curb and mowed down a row of mailboxes.
Machine guns had mowed down the first two waves.
Their closer mows down the bottom of the order every night.

entries.forms: mow /moʊ/ · mowed /moʊd/ · mown /moʊn/ · American usually mowed /moʊd/
entries.register: everyday — every American with a lawn says it weekly
entries.contrast: Americans say I have mowed the lawn; have mown reads as British. Mown does survive here as an adjective — newly mown grass, a mown field — and the fixed phrasal verb is always mowed down, never ✗ mown down, for people cut down by gunfire or a car. Rhymes with sow and sew, and splits its participles the same way.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; no stative or linking use anywhere in the entry.
entries.transitivity: both — the object is usual but optional: mow the yard, mow the back forty for hay, yet I mow every other Saturday is complete on its own.
entries.passive: yes — the crew has mowed the ball field twice this week → the ball field has been mowed twice this week; machine guns had mowed down the first two waves → the first two waves had been mowed down.

entries.meaning: To establish that something is true, or to turn out to be a certain way.
examples: Numbers by themselves don't prove much.
The prosecution never proved he was in the building.
She has proved every one of her critics wrong.
They only hire people with a proven track record.
The drive proved longer than the map suggested.
The drug had proved safe in two earlier trials.
That shortcut always proves to be slower.
Time proves most confident predictions wrong.
Rookies have to prove themselves all over again in the playoffs.
She has proved herself in three different departments.
He proved his doubters wrong in a single season.
You can prove it in two lines with induction.
Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem in the 1990s.
No one has proved the conjecture in either direction.
"The exception that proves the rule" uses the old sense, "tests."
The desert proved every part of the vehicle.
The estate had been proved in probate court that spring.
Let the dough prove in a warm spot for an hour.
The loaves had proved overnight in the cooler.

senses.head: Show something to be true
body: The core sense: evidence or argument that settles a question. In the perfect tense American prose prefers proved; proven is the form that goes in front of a noun — a proven method, proven reserves. The past is always proved: ✗ he proven it in court. (доказывать, подтверждать)
examples: Numbers by themselves don't prove much.
The prosecution never proved he was in the building.
She has proved every one of her critics wrong.
They only hire people with a proven track record.

senses.head: Turn out to be
body: A linking verb, followed by an adjective, a noun, or to be — the subject is not being demonstrated to anyone, it simply turns out a certain way. This sense has no passive: ✗ it was proved longer. (оказаться (каким-л.))
examples: The drive proved longer than the map suggested.
The drug had proved safe in two earlier trials.
That shortcut always proves to be slower.
Time proves most confident predictions wrong.

senses.head: prove oneself — show what one can do
body: Reflexive, about earning a reputation rather than establishing a fact. Also prove someone wrong, which is the commonest fixed pattern built on this verb. (проявить себя, показать, на что способен)
examples: Rookies have to prove themselves all over again in the playoffs.
She has proved herself in three different departments.
He proved his doubters wrong in a single season.

senses.head: Prove a theorem
body: The mathematical and logical sense: deriving a result from axioms or premises. Here proven is common in both slots — has proven, a proven result — more so than in ordinary prose. (доказывать (теорему, утверждение))
examples: You can prove it in two lines with induction.
Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem in the 1990s.
No one has proved the conjecture in either direction.

senses.head: Test, put to the test
body: The original sense, now archaic on its own but preserved in proving ground, in the saying the exception that proves the rule, and in the legal prove a will. (испытывать, проверять на прочность)
examples: "The exception that proves the rule" uses the old sense, "tests."
The desert proved every part of the vehicle.
The estate had been proved in probate court that spring.

senses.head: Rise, ferment (of dough)
body: Baking usage, chiefly British; American recipes normally say let it rise or, as a noun-derived verb, proof the dough. (подходить, подниматься (о тесте))
examples: Let the dough prove in a warm spot for an hour.
The loaves had proved overnight in the cooler.

entries.forms: prove /pruv/ · proved /pruvd/ · proven /ˈpruvən/ · the ordinary American participle is proved /pruvd/
entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Both participles are standard, and they divide the labor. In a perfect tense, edited American prose prefers proved: she has proved her point. Proven is the form that goes in front of a noun — a proven method, proven reserves — and it is frozen into the legal verdict not proven. The past tense is always proved: ✗ he proven it in court. See also disprove and reprove, which inherit the pattern.
entries.verb type: action in the demonstrating senses (prove a theorem, prove his doubters wrong), but linking (copular) in sense 2, turn out to be: the drive proved longer than the map suggested, the drug had proved safe.
entries.transitivity: transitive in the demonstrating senses, object obligatory (the prosecution never proved he was in the building), often with a following complement (proved his doubters wrong). The linking sense takes a subject complement and no object: that shortcut always proves to be slower.
entries.passive: restricted — yes in the demonstrating senses: no one has proved the conjecture, the estate had been proved in probate court. No passive of the linking sense: ✗ it was proved longer, ✗ safe was proved by the drug.

entries.meaning: To tell someone, formally and usually gently, that they have done something wrong.
examples: A good editor can reprove you without discouraging you.
The judge reproved both attorneys for talking over each other.
She has reproved him for the same habit more than once.
He had been reproved in front of the whole department.
The bishop reproved the practice in a letter to every parish.
Her silence reproves more effectively than any lecture.
The editorial has reproved the whole industry for looking away.
He gave me a reproving look and went back to his notes.

senses.head: Rebuke someone mildly
body: Formal and slightly old-fashioned; in speech Americans say scolded, called out, or chewed out. The participle is reproved — the -n form reproven is essentially unused, so never write ✗ has reproven. (упрекать, делать выговор, бранить)
examples: A good editor can reprove you without discouraging you.
The judge reproved both attorneys for talking over each other.
She has reproved him for the same habit more than once.
He had been reproved in front of the whole department.

senses.head: Condemn a practice or behavior
body: Here the object is conduct rather than a person, and the tone is public and moral. The participial adjective reproving — a reproving look, a reproving tone — belongs to this sense too. (порицать, осуждать (поступок, обычай))
examples: The bishop reproved the practice in a letter to every parish.
Her silence reproves more effectively than any lecture.
The editorial has reproved the whole industry for looking away.
He gave me a reproving look and went back to his notes.

entries.forms: reprove /rɪˈpruv/ · reproved /rɪˈpruvd/ · reproven /rɪˈpruvən/ · in American use the participle is reproved /rɪˈpruvd/
entries.register: rare — formal and old-fashioned; in speech Americans say scolded or called out
entries.contrast: The -n participle listed for this group, reproven, is essentially unused. Unlike prove, reprove has no attributive slot to keep it alive — there is no ✗ a reproven student — so write has reproved. The verb itself is formal and slightly old-fashioned; in speech Americans say scolded, called out, or chewed out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic verb of speech, formal in register; the participial adjective reproving (a reproving look) belongs to it.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is a person or a practice, and it is obligatory: reproved both attorneys, reproved the practice in a letter; ✗ the judge reproved alone is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes — he had been reproved in front of the whole department. Use reproved in the passive, never ✗ had been reproven.

entries.meaning: To split or tear something apart with violence — a verb you now meet almost only in its participle, riven.
examples: Old accounts use rive where we would say split or tear.
Lightning rived the oak from crown to root.
Frost has riven the ledge into loose slabs.
Every winter rives another crack in the foundation.
The congregation had been riven by the vote on the building fund.
A company riven by that kind of argument loses people fast.
The party has been riven over the same question for a decade.

senses.head: Split or tear apart violently
body: Archaic and literary in American English; ordinary prose uses split, tear, or crack. Watch the vowel: base and past have the long /aɪ/ of drive, but the participle riven shortens to /ˈrɪvən/ and rhymes with given. (раскалывать, расщеплять, разрывать)
examples: Old accounts use rive where we would say split or tear.
Lightning rived the oak from crown to root.
Frost has riven the ledge into loose slabs.
Every winter rives another crack in the foundation.

senses.head: riven — torn apart by conflict
body: The one fully current use, and it is participial: an institution riven by scandal, faction, or doubt. Written register, common in journalism. (раздираемый (расколом, конфликтом))
examples: The congregation had been riven by the vote on the building fund.
A company riven by that kind of argument loses people fast.
The party has been riven over the same question for a decade.

entries.forms: rive /raɪv/ · rived /raɪvd/ · riven /ˈrɪvən/
entries.register: archaic — the base verb is out of use; only riven survives, as an adjective
entries.contrast: Watch the vowel, because it is the one real surprise in this group: the base and past carry the long /aɪ/ of drive, but the participle riven shortens to /ˈrɪvən/ and rhymes with given. The base verb is now rare in American English; what survives is riven used adjectivally of something torn apart, usually an institution — a party riven by scandal. Compare writhe, another verb that lives on mainly in its most vivid form.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic verb of violent splitting. Archaic in the base and past; what survives is the participial adjective riven.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the thing torn apart: lightning rived the oak from crown to root, frost has riven the ledge into loose slabs.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is where the verb actually lives today: the congregation had been riven by the vote, the party has been riven over the same question for a decade.

entries.meaning: To decay, or to make something decay; also, of people and things, to be left neglected until they fall apart.
examples: Untreated fence posts rot within a few years.
The apples rotted on the ground before anyone picked them.
The floor had rotted through in two places.
Nobody wants a rotten board in a brand-new deck.
Water has rotted the sill under the window.
Damp rots wood faster than sun does.
Standing water rotted the roots within a month.
He can rot in there for all I care.
Two hundred boats were left to rot along the pier.
The proposal had rotted in a filing cabinet for years.
The whole system has rotted from the inside.
Discipline rotted under the third owner.
Institutions rot quietly long before anyone notices.

senses.head: Decay, go bad
body: The core intransitive sense, used of wood, fruit, meat, and cloth. Rotten is an adjective, not a working participle: write the boards have rotted, never ✗ the boards have rotten. (гнить, портиться, разлагаться)
examples: Untreated fence posts rot within a few years.
The apples rotted on the ground before anyone picked them.
The floor had rotted through in two places.
Nobody wants a rotten board in a brand-new deck.

senses.head: Cause something to decay
body: The transitive twin of the first sense, with damp, water, sugar, or salt as the subject. (гноить, вызывать гниение)
examples: Water has rotted the sill under the window.
Damp rots wood faster than sun does.
Standing water rotted the roots within a month.

senses.head: Be left to languish
body: Figurative, of a person shut away or a thing abandoned: rot in jail, left to rot. Carries anger or contempt, so it is not a neutral choice. (гнить, чахнуть, пропадать (в тюрьме, без дела))
examples: He can rot in there for all I care.
Two hundred boats were left to rot along the pier.
The proposal had rotted in a filing cabinet for years.

senses.head: Decay morally or institutionally
body: Of a system, a culture, or an organization losing its integrity from within. Usually paired with from the inside or at the core; the adjective is rotten (rotten to the core). (разлагаться, прогнить)
examples: The whole system has rotted from the inside.
Discipline rotted under the third owner.
Institutions rot quietly long before anyone notices.

entries.forms: rot /rɑt/ · rotted /ˈrɑtɪd/ · rotten /ˈrɑtən/ · the working American participle is rotted /ˈrɑtɪd/
entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Rotten is an adjective, not a working participle: write the boards have rotted, never ✗ the boards have rotten. Use rotten in front of a noun (a rotten plank, rotten luck) or after be (the milk is rotten). Exactly the division you see in melt and molten. Note the American vowel, /ɑ/, not the British /ɒ/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic process verb, fine in the progressive (the posts are rotting); ergative like melt. Rotten is an adjective, not a working participle: ✗ the boards have rotten.
entries.transitivity: both — chiefly intransitive (the apples rotted on the ground, he can rot in there), transitive only with damp, water, or sugar as the causer: water has rotted the sill under the window.
entries.passive: restricted — the causative use passivizes weakly, and was rotted there reads half-adjectival: the sill had been rotted by years of runoff. The intransitive senses have no passive: ✗ the apples were rotted on the ground.

entries.meaning: To cut something with a saw, or to move back and forth the way a saw does. Note that saw is also the past tense of see — a different verb entirely.
examples: Saw the boards to length before you carry them upstairs.
He sawed the branch off flush with the trunk.
I have sawed through this whole stack twice already.
The mill saws two hundred logs a day.
British lumberyards advertise sawn timber; American ones say dimensional lumber.
They sawed off the legs to fit the table under the window.
Someone had sawed off the padlock overnight.
A sawed-off shotgun is illegal in most states.
He sawed at the steak with a butter knife.
The fiddler saws away for three hours straight.
She had sawed at the rope until her hands blistered.
He was sawing logs on the couch by nine.
Dad saws logs loud enough to hear from the driveway.

senses.head: Cut with a saw
body: The literal sense. The -n participle is British: Americans write has sawed and sawed-off, where British English has sawn and sawn-off. Do not confuse this verb with the past of see: ✗ I sawed a movie last night. (пилить, распиливать)
examples: Saw the boards to length before you carry them upstairs.
He sawed the branch off flush with the trunk.
I have sawed through this whole stack twice already.
The mill saws two hundred logs a day.
British lumberyards advertise sawn timber; American ones say dimensional lumber.

senses.head: saw off — cut off; sawed-off
body: A common phrasal use, and the source of the fixed adjective sawed-off — a shortened shotgun, and, jokingly, a very short person. (отпиливать; обрезанный, укороченный (об оружии))
examples: They sawed off the legs to fit the table under the window.
Someone had sawed off the padlock overnight.
A sawed-off shotgun is illegal in most states.

senses.head: Move back and forth like a saw
body: Of hacking at something with a dull blade, or — with away at — of playing a bowed instrument energetically and not very well. (пилить (движением взад-вперёд); водить смычком)
examples: He sawed at the steak with a butter knife.
The fiddler saws away for three hours straight.
She had sawed at the rope until her hands blistered.

senses.head: saw logs — snore
body: American slang, always in this fixed phrase and usually in the progressive. (храпеть (разг.))
examples: He was sawing logs on the couch by nine.
Dad saws logs loud enough to hear from the driveway.

entries.forms: saw /sɔ/ · sawed /sɔd/ · sawn /sɔn/ · the American participle is sawed /sɔd/
entries.register: everyday — ordinary in the shop, in the yard, and figuratively
entries.contrast: Two traps here. First, saw is also the past tense of see, and the two verbs have nothing to do with each other: ✗ I sawed a movie last night should be I saw a movie. That other saw carries a trap of its own, and it is the commonest verb error in American speech: see runs see — saw — seen, so the past stands alone (I saw it) and the participle needs a helper (I have seen it) — never the bare ✗ I seen it. Second, the -n participle is British: Americans write has sawed and a sawed-off shotgun where British English has sawn and sawn-off. Compare whipsaw, built directly on this verb, and gnaw.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. Note that the base is also the past of see, an unrelated verb: ✗ I sawed a movie last night wants I saw a movie.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (sawed the branch off flush with the trunk, the mill saws two hundred logs a day), intransitive with at or away (he sawed at the steak with a butter knife, the fiddler saws away for three hours).
entries.passive: restricted — yes for the transitive senses: someone had sawed off the padlock → the padlock had been sawed off overnight. No passive of saw at the steak or of the slang saw logs: ✗ logs were being sawed by Dad is not the idiom.

entries.meaning: To join, make, or mend things with a needle and thread.
examples: She can sew a straight seam faster than a machine.
The costumes had been sewn by volunteers.
My grandmother sews every curtain in the house.
She sewed her own wedding dress.
I have sewn three of these jackets and the lining still puckers.
He sews costumes for the community theater.
He sewed the button back on during the meeting.
Can you sew up this tear before Friday?
Someone has sewn a patch over the hole in the elbow.
The resident sewed the cut closed in about four minutes.
The gash had been sewn shut before I even felt it.
By March they had the contract sewed up.
One more win sews up the division.
The defense had sewed up the case by Wednesday.

senses.head: Stitch cloth together
body: The core sense, by hand or by machine. Both participles are standard in American English, with sewn the commoner in edited prose. Pronounced like so and like sow — /soʊ/, never ✗ /su/. (шить, сшивать)
examples: She can sew a straight seam faster than a machine.
The costumes had been sewn by volunteers.
My grandmother sews every curtain in the house.

senses.head: Make a garment by sewing
body: With the finished thing as the object rather than the cloth. Often contrasted with buying something ready-made. (шить (одежду), пошить)
examples: She sewed her own wedding dress.
I have sewn three of these jackets and the lining still puckers.
He sews costumes for the community theater.

senses.head: Attach or mend by stitching
body: Sew on a button, sew up a tear, sew a patch over a hole. The repair sense, and the one most people use most often. (пришивать, зашивать, штопать)
examples: He sewed the button back on during the meeting.
Can you sew up this tear before Friday?
Someone has sewn a patch over the hole in the elbow.

senses.head: Close a wound with stitches
body: The medical use, normally sew up or sew shut. In clinical writing suture is the technical verb, but sew is what everyone says. (зашивать (рану))
examples: The resident sewed the cut closed in about four minutes.
The gash had been sewn shut before I even felt it.

senses.head: sew up — settle, secure
body: An idiom for making an outcome certain — a contract, an election, a division title. This one always takes sewed up, not ✗ sewn up, in American usage. (обеспечить, решить дело, закрыть вопрос)
examples: By March they had the contract sewed up.
One more win sews up the division.
The defense had sewed up the case by Wednesday.

entries.forms: sew /soʊ/ · sewed /soʊd/ · sewn /soʊn/ · American also sewed /soʊd/
entries.register: everyday — an ordinary household verb
entries.contrast: Pronounced exactly like sow and like so — /soʊ/, never ✗ /su/. Both participles are standard American, with sewn the commoner in edited prose; but the idiom takes sewed: they have the election sewed up, not ✗ sewn up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; no stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — the object is usually present (sew a straight seam, sew the button back on, sew up this tear), but drops freely when the skill is the point: she can sew.
entries.passive: yes — the costumes had been sewn by volunteers, the gash had been sewn shut. The settle, secure idiom takes sewed: by March they had the contract sewed up, not ✗ sewn up.

entries.meaning: To give something a form with your hands or by force, or to influence how something turns out.
examples: Bakers shape the loaves by hand every morning.
The wind shaped the dunes into long parallel ridges.
He shapes the clay with his thumbs, not with tools.
The fruit was small and misshapen, but it tasted fine.
Two teachers shape most of what a kid believes about school.
That one summer has shaped every decision I've made since.
The policy had been shaped by a single lawsuit.
He shaped up fast once the coach benched him.
You need to shape up or find another crew.
She has shaped up considerably since the review.
This is shaping up to be the driest June on record.
The season shaped up better than anyone expected.

senses.head: Give something a physical form
body: Working clay, dough, metal, or land into a form. Shape is fully regular today; the old participle shapen survives in exactly one word, the adjective misshapen, and never write ✗ has shapen. (придавать форму, лепить, формовать)
examples: Bakers shape the loaves by hand every morning.
The wind shaped the dunes into long parallel ridges.
He shapes the clay with his thumbs, not with tools.
The fruit was small and misshapen, but it tasted fine.

senses.head: Influence how something develops
body: The commonest sense in writing: an experience, a law, or a person that determines the course of something. Frequently passive — shaped by. (формировать, определять, влиять на)
examples: Two teachers shape most of what a kid believes about school.
That one summer has shaped every decision I've made since.
The policy had been shaped by a single lawsuit.

senses.head: shape up — improve, get in line
body: Informal, of behavior or physical condition getting better. The warning shape up or ship out is fixed. (взяться за ум, исправиться; привести себя в форму)
examples: He shaped up fast once the coach benched him.
You need to shape up or find another crew.
She has shaped up considerably since the review.

senses.head: shape up — develop, turn out
body: A different meaning of the same phrasal verb: how a season, a plan, or a situation is heading. Nearly always progressive — is shaping up to be. (складываться, вырисовываться)
examples: This is shaping up to be the driest June on record.
The season shaped up better than anyone expected.

entries.forms: shape /ʃeɪp/ · shaped /ʃeɪpt/ · shapen /ˈʃeɪpən/ · the American participle is shaped /ʃeɪpt/
entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Shape is fully regular today, and shapen survives in exactly one word — the adjective misshapen — and nowhere else. Never write ✗ has shapen. Note also that the written -d of shaped is pronounced /t/, because p is voiceless.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both the physical sense (shape the loaves) and the influencing sense (that summer shaped every decision); shape up is dynamic too.
entries.transitivity: transitive in the main senses, object obligatory (the wind shaped the dunes; ✗ bakers shape every morning is incomplete). The phrasal shape up is intransitive: he shaped up fast, this is shaping up to be the driest June on record.
entries.passive: yes, and the influencing sense is frequently passive: the policy had been shaped by a single lawsuit. Never ✗ has shapen — the -n form survives only inside misshapen.

entries.meaning: To cut hair off the skin with a razor, or to take a thin layer or a small amount off something.
examples: I shave every other morning at most.
He shaved his beard off the day after the season ended.
She has shaved her head every summer since high school.
The new manager was young, clean-shaven, and visibly nervous.
The carpenter had shaved an eighth of an inch off the door.
Shave the chocolate over the top with a peeler.
He shaves the reed until it plays cleanly.
He shaves a few seconds off his time every week.
They shaved four dollars off the ticket price.
We have shaved two weeks off the schedule already.
The bus shaved the curb taking the corner.
His shot had shaved the post and gone wide.
Two starters admitted they shaved points that season.
Investigators showed the team had shaved points in four games.

senses.head: Remove hair with a razor
body: The everyday sense, transitive or with no object at all. Use shaved in the perfect: he has shaved his head since college. Shaven is an adjective and lives inside compounds — clean-shaven, close-shaven, freshly shaven. (брить, бриться)
examples: I shave every other morning at most.
He shaved his beard off the day after the season ended.
She has shaved her head every summer since high school.
The new manager was young, clean-shaven, and visibly nervous.

senses.head: Take a thin layer off something
body: Carpentry and cooking: paring material away in thin slices with a plane, a knife, or a peeler. (снимать тонкий слой, строгать, состругивать)
examples: The carpenter had shaved an eighth of an inch off the door.
Shave the chocolate over the top with a peeler.
He shaves the reed until it plays cleanly.

senses.head: Reduce by a small amount
body: Figurative, always with off or from and a small quantity: seconds, dollars, percentage points, weeks of a schedule. (срезать, сократить (время, расходы, цену))
examples: He shaves a few seconds off his time every week.
They shaved four dollars off the ticket price.
We have shaved two weeks off the schedule already.

senses.head: Graze, pass very close to
body: Less common, and mostly journalistic: a vehicle or a ball passing so close that it barely touches. The related noun is a close shave. (пройти впритирку, чиркнуть, задеть)
examples: The bus shaved the curb taking the corner.
His shot had shaved the post and gone wide.

senses.head: shave points — fix a score
body: American sports-betting term: players deliberately keep the margin of victory under the point spread. Always in this fixed phrase. (намеренно занижать счёт (в спорте, ради ставок))
examples: Two starters admitted they shaved points that season.
Investigators showed the team had shaved points in four games.

entries.forms: shave /ʃeɪv/ · shaved /ʃeɪvd/ · shaven /ˈʃeɪvən/ · the American participle is shaved /ʃeɪvd/
entries.register: everyday — a daily verb for most of the country
entries.contrast: For the perfect tense use shaved: he has shaved his head since college. Shaven is an adjective and lives almost entirely inside compounds — clean-shaven, close-shaven, freshly shaven — so ✗ he has shaven sounds wrong to American ears. Compare shape and grave, two more verbs whose -n form is now purely adjectival.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; no stative or linking use. Shaven is an adjective (clean-shaven), not a working participle.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shaved his beard off, shaved four dollars off the ticket price, the bus shaved the curb), intransitive with no object at all: I shave every other morning at most.
entries.passive: yes — the reed is shaved until it plays cleanly, points had been shaved in four games. Use shaved in the perfect and passive: ✗ he has shaven sounds wrong to American ears.

entries.meaning: An old spelling of show, pronounced the same way — /ʃoʊ/ — and meaning the same thing; you meet it in the King James Bible and in older books and legal forms.
examples: Older printings shew the word where a modern edition prints show.
The 1611 translators shewed a clear preference for this spelling.
Editors have shewn it that way in every reprint of the text.
The old ledger shews every payment in a clerk's careful hand.
That psalm asks the Lord to shew mercy.
The chronicler shewed forth the whole history of the kings.
The manuscript had shewn the same reading before the page was damaged.

senses.head: Archaic spelling of show
body: Not a separate verb: it is show in its old dress, and it was never pronounced ✗ /ʃu/ to rhyme with few. In anything you write yourself, use show. (показывать (устаревшее написание))
examples: Older printings shew the word where a modern edition prints show.
The 1611 translators shewed a clear preference for this spelling.
Editors have shewn it that way in every reprint of the text.
The old ledger shews every payment in a clerk's careful hand.

senses.head: shew mercy, shew forth — grant, display
body: Biblical fixed phrases, the context in which most readers actually meet the spelling. Purely liturgical or literary register now. (являть, оказывать (милость); возвещать)
examples: That psalm asks the Lord to shew mercy.
The chronicler shewed forth the whole history of the kings.
The manuscript had shewn the same reading before the page was damaged.

entries.forms: shew /ʃoʊ/ · shewed /ʃoʊd/ · shewn /ʃoʊn/ · the modern spelling is show — showed — shown
entries.register: archaic — an old spelling of show, met in the King James Bible and older books
entries.contrast: Shew is not a separate verb — it is an old spelling of show, and it was always pronounced the same way, /ʃoʊ/, never ✗ /ʃu/ to rhyme with few. You will meet it in the King James Bible, in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century books, and on old legal forms. In anything you write yourself, use show.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, exactly like show; this is an old spelling of that verb, not a separate one. Archaic register only.
entries.transitivity: ditransitive, as show is — shew mercy to the people, shew someone the way — and plain transitive elsewhere: the old ledger shews every payment.
entries.passive: yes, on the same terms as show — editors have shewn it that way in every reprint, the manuscript had shewn the same reading. In anything you write yourself, use show.

entries.meaning: To let someone see something — and from there to demonstrate, guide, teach, reveal, be visible, or turn up.
examples: Let me show you where the fuse box is.
He showed his ID at the door and walked straight in.
She has shown me that same photograph four times.
Both witnesses were shown the same lineup.
The data shows a steady drop since March.
The audit showed no missing funds.
Two later studies have shown the opposite.
An usher will show you to your seat.
She showed us around the plant for an hour.
They had shown him out before he finished the sentence.
Show me how you tie that knot.
He showed the whole crew the shortcut in five minutes.
Nobody had shown him how the machine worked.
He never shows frustration on the mound.
The patient showed no signs of infection.
She has shown nothing but patience with him.
The stain doesn't show under the rug.
His nerves showed the whole first period.
The patch has faded so much it barely shows now.
The museum is showing forty of her drawings.
They showed the film twice a night all summer.
Her work has been shown in three cities.
Half the team never showed up.
He has shown up late to every rehearsal.
Nobody shows up to those meetings anymore.
He shows off every time there's a camera.
She showed off the new car for a solid ten minutes.
They have shown off that kitchen to everyone who visits.
The intern showed up three senior analysts at the whiteboard.
He hates being shown up in front of his kids.

senses.head: Let someone see something
body: The core sense, with two objects: show me the photo, show the photo to me. The past is showed, the participle is shown: ✗ he has showed me the file wants has shown, and ✗ he shown me the file wants showed. (показывать, предъявлять)
examples: Let me show you where the fuse box is.
He showed his ID at the door and walked straight in.
She has shown me that same photograph four times.
Both witnesses were shown the same lineup.

senses.head: Demonstrate, be evidence of
body: With data, research, a record, or a result as the subject. The standard verb of scientific and news writing: the study shows that… (показывать, свидетельствовать, доказывать)
examples: The data shows a steady drop since March.
The audit showed no missing funds.
Two later studies have shown the opposite.

senses.head: Guide, lead someone somewhere
body: Always with a direction word: show someone in, out, around, to their seat, up the stairs. (проводить, отвести, показать дорогу)
examples: An usher will show you to your seat.
She showed us around the plant for an hour.
They had shown him out before he finished the sentence.

senses.head: Teach by demonstrating
body: Usually show someone how to do something — teaching by doing it in front of them rather than explaining. (научить, показать (как что-л. делать))
examples: Show me how you tie that knot.
He showed the whole crew the shortcut in five minutes.
Nobody had shown him how the machine worked.

senses.head: Reveal a feeling or quality
body: Of a person letting an emotion appear, or of a body, a machine, or a patient showing signs of something. Often negative: never shows any nerves. (проявлять, выказывать, обнаруживать)
examples: He never shows frustration on the mound.
The patient showed no signs of infection.
She has shown nothing but patience with him.

senses.head: Be visible
body: Intransitive, with no object — a stain, a repair, a seam, or a feeling that can be seen. Also of pregnancy: she's starting to show. (быть заметным, виднеться, проступать)
examples: The stain doesn't show under the rug.
His nerves showed the whole first period.
The patch has faded so much it barely shows now.

senses.head: Exhibit or screen
body: Of a gallery hanging work, a theater running a film, or an artist having work exhibited. Frequently passive: her work has been shown in three cities. (выставлять; демонстрировать, показывать (фильм))
examples: The museum is showing forty of her drawings.
They showed the film twice a night all summer.
Her work has been shown in three cities.

senses.head: show up — arrive, appear
body: Informal but extremely common; also of a thing becoming detectable — the crack showed up on the X-ray. (появиться, объявиться, прийти)
examples: Half the team never showed up.
He has shown up late to every rehearsal.
Nobody shows up to those meetings anymore.

senses.head: show off — display to impress
body: Intransitive of a person behaving boastfully, transitive of the thing being displayed. Mildly disapproving; the noun is a show-off. (выпендриваться, хвастаться, красоваться)
examples: He shows off every time there's a camera.
She showed off the new car for a solid ten minutes.
They have shown off that kitchen to everyone who visits.

senses.head: show someone up — outdo, embarrass
body: The object goes between the verb and up. Distinct from show up meaning "arrive" — here someone is made to look bad by comparison. (утереть нос, выставить в невыгодном свете)
examples: The intern showed up three senior analysts at the whiteboard.
He hates being shown up in front of his kids.

entries.forms: show /ʃoʊ/ · showed /ʃoʊd/ · shown /ʃoʊn/
entries.register: everyday — one of the most common verbs in the language
entries.contrast: This is the one verb in the group that American English will not let you treat as regular, and it is the group's real workhorse. The past is showed, the participle is shown: ✗ He has showed me the file wants has shown. Run the swap the other way and it is just as wrong: ✗ He shown me the file wants the plain past, showed. Compare shew, which is this same verb in its old dress.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. Sense 6, be visible, is closer to a state but still takes the progressive (she's starting to show), so it is not a true stative.
entries.transitivity: ditransitive and more — two objects (show me the photo / show the photo to me), plain transitive (the audit showed no missing funds), and intransitive in the be visible sense (the stain doesn't show under the rug).
entries.passive: yes, and either object can become the subject: both witnesses were shown the same lineup, her work has been shown in three cities, he hates being shown up in front of his kids. No passive of the intransitive the stain doesn't show.
entries.phrasal verbs: show around · show in · show off · show out · show up

entries.meaning: To scatter seed on ground so it will grow — and, figuratively, to plant an idea or a feeling that will grow later.
examples: We sow the cover crop right after the last harvest.
He sowed rye across the whole back field.
The wind has sown thistle along every fence line.
She sows the small plots by hand.
They sowed the north forty in clover.
A field sown in late October comes up thin.
The terraces had been sown with barley for centuries.
Doubt had been sown long before the vote.
Those rumors sow confusion on purpose.
The memo sowed panic in half the building.
He sowed his wild oats and then settled down fast.
Everybody's entitled to sow a few wild oats.

senses.head: Plant seed
body: The core farming sense, with the seed or crop as the object. Rhymes with go, /soʊ/ — the noun sow meaning a female pig is a different word, /saʊ/. Both participles are standard, but sown is the usual American choice. (сеять, высевать)
examples: We sow the cover crop right after the last harvest.
He sowed rye across the whole back field.
The wind has sown thistle along every fence line.
She sows the small plots by hand.

senses.head: Plant a field with a crop
body: The same action seen from the other end: the ground is the object, and the crop follows with in or with. (засевать (поле, участок))
examples: They sowed the north forty in clover.
A field sown in late October comes up thin.
The terraces had been sown with barley for centuries.

senses.head: Spread an idea or feeling
body: Figurative, and almost always something unwelcome — doubt, discord, confusion, panic. Sown is nearly automatic here. The proverb as you sow, so shall you reap belongs to this sense. (сеять, посеять (сомнение, раздор, панику))
examples: Doubt had been sown long before the vote.
Those rumors sow confusion on purpose.
The memo sowed panic in half the building.

senses.head: sow one's wild oats
body: A fixed idiom about reckless behavior in youth, followed by settling down. Traditionally said of young men, and dated in tone. (перебеситься в молодости, нагуляться)
examples: He sowed his wild oats and then settled down fast.
Everybody's entitled to sow a few wild oats.

entries.forms: sow /soʊ/ · sowed /soʊd/ · sown /soʊn/ · American also sowed /soʊd/
entries.register: everyday — ordinary in farming and in the figurative sow doubt, as you sow, so shall you reap
entries.contrast: Two different words share this spelling. The verb here rhymes with go — /soʊ/ — and means "plant seed"; the noun sow, a female pig, rhymes with now, /saʊ/. Both participles are standard American, but sown is the usual one, and it is nearly automatic in the figurative sense: doubt sown early. Sounds identical to sew.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the farming sense and in the figurative sow doubt alike; no stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with either the seed or the ground as object: sowed rye across the whole back field, sowed the north forty in clover. The object drops when the method is the point: she sows by hand.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual shape of the figurative sense: doubt had been sown long before the vote; also the terraces had been sown with barley for centuries.

entries.meaning: To scatter things loosely over a surface so that they lie spread around.
examples: They strew sawdust on the floor before every show.
The storm strewed branches across both lanes of the highway.
Someone has strewn gravel all over the walkway.
She strews wildflower seed along the ditch every spring.
The room had been strewn with unopened mail for weeks.
Papers lay strewn across every surface in the office.
The shoulder of the road was strewn with glass.
His career is strewn with abandoned projects.
Every draft he strews with footnotes nobody can follow.
The report had been strewn with numbers no one could source.

senses.head: Scatter things over a surface
body: The active sense: sawdust on a floor, petals on an aisle, gravel on a walk. Unlike most of this group, strew keeps its -n participle firmly in American English; strewed is acceptable but uncommon. (разбрасывать, посыпать, усыпать)
examples: They strew sawdust on the floor before every show.
The storm strewed branches across both lanes of the highway.
Someone has strewn gravel all over the walkway.
She strews wildflower seed along the ditch every spring.

senses.head: be strewn with — lie covered in
body: The passive is the commonest shape of this verb. The surface becomes the subject and the scattered things follow with with: the floor was strewn with paper. (быть усыпанным, усеянным (чем-л.))
examples: The room had been strewn with unopened mail for weeks.
Papers lay strewn across every surface in the office.
The shoulder of the road was strewn with glass.

senses.head: Figurative — dotted with, full of
body: Of a text, a career, or a record marked all over with something — errors, references, abandoned projects. Written register. (изобиловать, быть усеянным (ошибками, отсылками))
examples: His career is strewn with abandoned projects.
Every draft he strews with footnotes nobody can follow.
The report had been strewn with numbers no one could source.

entries.forms: strew /stru/ · strewed /strud/ · strewn /strun/
entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing, especially strewn, less common in speech
entries.contrast: Unlike most of this group, strew keeps its -n participle firmly in American English: the floor was strewn with paper, not ✗ strewed with paper. Strewed is acceptable but uncommon. Watch the vowel — /stru/, like true, with no /j/ glide, unlike hew /hju/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic verb of scattering. Unlike most of this group it keeps a live -n participle: strewn, not ✗ strewed with paper.
entries.transitivity: transitive — either the scattered things (they strew sawdust on the floor) or the covered surface (every draft he strews with footnotes) can be the object.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the commonest shape of the verb: the shoulder of the road was strewn with glass, his career is strewn with abandoned projects.

entries.meaning: To get bigger — by puffing up, expanding, rising in number, or growing louder.
examples: Bee stings swell more than they hurt.
His ankle swelled within minutes.
Her knee has swollen to twice its normal size.
He walked in with a swollen lip and would not say why.
The crowd swelled after the second band came on.
Membership swells every January and drops off by March.
Enrollment has swelled by a third since 2019.
The creek had swollen over the low bridge by dawn.
Every river in the county swells after a week like that.
The channel swelled with runoff for three days.
The strings swell under the last line of dialogue.
The chorus swelled until it filled the room.
The noise had swelled into something you could feel.
Applause has swelled every night this week.
His chest swelled when they read her name.
Pride had swelled in him all evening.
Two good reviews have swelled his head considerably.
Wooden doors swell in humid weather.
The beans swelled to twice their size overnight.
The frame had swollen shut after a week of rain.

senses.head: Puff up (of the body)
body: Injury, infection, or an allergic reaction. This is the sense that takes swollen: my ankle has swollen, a swollen lip. The past is always swelled — ✗ my ankle swollen overnight. (опухать, отекать, распухать)
examples: Bee stings swell more than they hurt.
His ankle swelled within minutes.
Her knee has swollen to twice its normal size.
He walked in with a swollen lip and would not say why.

senses.head: Grow in number or size
body: Of a crowd, a budget, membership, or a population. Growth in quantity normally takes swelled rather than swollen. (расти, увеличиваться (в числе, в объёме))
examples: The crowd swelled after the second band came on.
Membership swells every January and drops off by March.
Enrollment has swelled by a third since 2019.

senses.head: Rise, run high (of water)
body: Of a river or the sea rising above its normal level. The related noun a swell is the long rolling wave that follows a storm. (подниматься, вздуваться (о реке, о море))
examples: The creek had swollen over the low bridge by dawn.
Every river in the county swells after a week like that.
The channel swelled with runoff for three days.

senses.head: Grow louder (of sound)
body: Of music, applause, or noise building gradually. Common in writing about performance; the musical noun is a swell. (нарастать, усиливаться (о звуке))
examples: The strings swell under the last line of dialogue.
The chorus swelled until it filled the room.
The noise had swelled into something you could feel.
Applause has swelled every night this week.

senses.head: Fill with emotion
body: Of a chest or a heart filling with pride, love, or anger. The fixed a swelled head means conceit, and takes swelled, not swollen. (переполняться (гордостью, чувством))
examples: His chest swelled when they read her name.
Pride had swelled in him all evening.
Two good reviews have swelled his head considerably.

senses.head: Expand from moisture
body: Of wood, seeds, beans, or paper taking up water and growing. Everyday practical usage. (разбухать, набухать)
examples: Wooden doors swell in humid weather.
The beans swelled to twice their size overnight.
The frame had swollen shut after a week of rain.

entries.forms: swell /swɛl/ · swelled /swɛld/ · swollen /ˈswoʊlən/ · American also swelled /swɛld/
entries.register: everyday — ordinary of injuries, crowds, and rivers
entries.contrast: Both participles are standard, and Americans sort them by sense. Physical swelling takes swollen: my ankle has swollen, a swollen river. Growth in number, volume, or pride usually takes swelled: the crowd has swelled to ten thousand, a swelled head. The past tense is always swelled: ✗ my ankle swollen overnight needs swelled. This is the group's healthiest -en participle; compare melt, where the same old ending died off entirely.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic process verb, fine in the progressive (the crowd is swelling). Not stative, despite the resultant adjective swollen.
entries.transitivity: both — overwhelmingly intransitive (his ankle swelled within minutes, the chorus swelled until it filled the room), transitive only with an external causer: two good reviews have swelled his head, runoff swelled the channel.
entries.passive: restricted, effectively no — the transitive use passivizes badly and was swollen reads as an adjective rather than an action: ✗ his head was swelled by two good reviews. The intransitive senses have no passive at all.

entries.meaning: To grow larger or stronger — said of the moon, and of moods, fashions, and reputations — and, in the everyday sense, to apply wax to something.
examples: The moon waxed all week toward Friday's full.
A waxing crescent is easiest to see just after sunset.
The moon has waxed and waned twice since we started counting.
His influence has waxed and waned twice in ten years.
Interest in the case waxes every time a new document surfaces.
Enthusiasm had waxed considerably by the second rehearsal.
Critics still wax nostalgic about the first two albums.
He waxed poetic about a sandwich for ten minutes.
She has waxed eloquent on this subject before.
I wax the car twice a year.
She waxed the floors before the open house.
They have waxed these boards every fall since 1970.
She waxes her own eyebrows.
The salon waxed both her arms in twenty minutes.
I have never waxed anything in my life.
She lay very still, her face waxen in the lamplight.

senses.head: Grow bigger (of the moon)
body: The lit face of the moon growing from new toward full. Its opposite is wane, and the pair is fixed: waxed and waned. The verb is regular — the moon has waxed, never ✗ has waxen. (прибывать (о Луне))
examples: The moon waxed all week toward Friday's full.
A waxing crescent is easiest to see just after sunset.
The moon has waxed and waned twice since we started counting.

senses.head: Increase, grow stronger
body: Of influence, enthusiasm, or interest. Formal and slightly literary; usually paired with wane, and rarely used alone in speech. (расти, усиливаться, крепнуть)
examples: His influence has waxed and waned twice in ten years.
Interest in the case waxes every time a new document surfaces.
Enthusiasm had waxed considerably by the second rehearsal.

senses.head: wax poetic, wax nostalgic — become
body: A linking use surviving in a handful of fixed collocations — wax poetic, lyrical, eloquent, nostalgic, philosophical — and usually with a light touch of mockery. You cannot extend it freely: ✗ he waxed angry. (становиться (лирическим, ностальгическим), пускаться в (рассуждения))
examples: Critics still wax nostalgic about the first two albums.
He waxed poetic about a sandwich for ten minutes.
She has waxed eloquent on this subject before.

senses.head: Polish or coat with wax
body: The ordinary modern sense, unrelated in feel to the growing one but the same regular verb: cars, floors, skis, surfboards. (натирать воском, вощить)
examples: I wax the car twice a year.
She waxed the floors before the open house.
They have waxed these boards every fall since 1970.

senses.head: Remove hair with wax
body: Salon usage, transitive with the body part or the person as the object. The related noun is a wax. (делать восковую депиляцию)
examples: She waxes her own eyebrows.
The salon waxed both her arms in twenty minutes.
I have never waxed anything in my life.
She lay very still, her face waxen in the lamplight.

entries.forms: wax /wæks/ · waxed /wækst/ · waxen /ˈwæksən/ · the American participle is waxed /wækst/
entries.register: everyday — waxing the car, waxing a floor, a waxing moon; only waxen is literary
entries.third person: waxes (-es after x) · -ing form: waxing (no spelling change)
entries.contrast: The verb is regular today: the moon has waxed, never ✗ has waxen. Waxen survives only as an adjective meaning "pale and stiff, like wax" — a waxen face. Its opposite is wane, and the pair is fixed: waxed and waned. This is the same regular verb as the everyday wax meaning "polish" or "remove hair." Compare melt: another -en form stranded as an adjective.
entries.verb type: action in the growing sense (the moon waxed all week) and in the polishing and depilation senses; linking (copular) in the fixed wax poetic / lyrical / eloquent / nostalgic, meaning become — and it will not extend past those collocations: ✗ he waxed angry.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the moon and influence senses (his influence has waxed and waned) and in the linking use; transitive in the everyday senses: I wax the car twice a year, she waxes her own eyebrows.
entries.passive: restricted — yes for the apply wax and remove hair senses: the floors were waxed before the open house, both her arms were waxed in twenty minutes. No passive of the growing sense (it is intransitive) or of the linking one: ✗ nostalgic was waxed by the critics.

entries.meaning: To hurt someone from two directions at once — and, literally, to cut with a long two-handled saw.
examples: Rising rates and falling rents whipsawed small landlords last year.
The team had been whipsawed by injuries on both lines.
A thin market whipsaws anyone who trades on momentum.
Traders have been whipsawed by three straight reversals.
The index whipsawed between gains and losses all afternoon.
Two workers whipsaw a log from opposite ends of the blade.
They had whipsawed every timber in the barn by hand.
Old mill records describe the planks as whipsawn rather than milled.

senses.head: Hit from two directions at once
body: The living American sense, a staple of business and sports writing, and usually passive: costs rising while revenue falls, injuries on both lines. Built on saw and following it in everything, including the American preference for whipsawed over British-flavored whipsawn. (бить с двух сторон, зажимать в тиски (обстоятельств))
examples: Rising rates and falling rents whipsawed small landlords last year.
The team had been whipsawed by injuries on both lines.
A thin market whipsaws anyone who trades on momentum.

senses.head: Be caught by market reversals
body: The specific trading sense: a price that reverses just after you act, so you lose on both the entry and the exit. Nearly always passive — whipsawed by. (выбить стоп-лоссы резкими разворотами (о рынке))
examples: Traders have been whipsawed by three straight reversals.
The index whipsawed between gains and losses all afternoon.

senses.head: Cut with a two-handled saw
body: The literal woodworking sense, worked by two people pulling in turn. Nearly obsolete outside historical and milling contexts. (пилить продольной (лучковой) пилой)
examples: Two workers whipsaw a log from opposite ends of the blade.
They had whipsawed every timber in the barn by hand.
Old mill records describe the planks as whipsawn rather than milled.

entries.forms: whipsaw /ˈwɪpsɔ/ · whipsawed /ˈwɪpsɔd/ · whipsawn /ˈwɪpsɔn/ · the American participle is whipsawed /ˈwɪpsɔd/
entries.register: rare — a business-page verb built on saw; the literal woodworking sense is dead
entries.contrast: Built on saw and following it in everything, including the American preference for whipsawed over the British-flavored whipsawn. Worth knowing that the literal woodworking sense is nearly dead; what Americans actually use is the figurative one — to be whipsawed is to take losses from two directions at once, a staple of business and sports writing.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the living American sense is figurative (hit from two directions at once), the literal woodworking one nearly obsolete.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the person, team, or market caught from both sides: rising rates and falling rents whipsawed small landlords last year.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the normal form: the team had been whipsawed by injuries on both lines, traders have been whipsawed by three straight reversals. American English uses whipsawed, not ✗ whipsawn.

entries.meaning: To twist the body, usually from pain or acute embarrassment.
examples: Burn patients writhe even under sedation.
He writhed on the field for a full minute before the trainer reached him.
The patient had writhed all night before the medication took hold.
He writhes visibly whenever anyone brings up the old commercial.
She has writhed through worse interviews than that one.
I writhed in my seat for the whole toast.
Snakes writhe when you pin them behind the head.
Smoke writhed up from the pile all afternoon.
Old poems describe writhen roots gripping the bare rock.

senses.head: Twist in pain
body: The core sense. The w is silent and the th is the voiced /ð/ of bathe, not the /θ/ of both. American English uses has writhed; ✗ has writhen is archaic. (корчиться, извиваться (от боли))
examples: Burn patients writhe even under sedation.
He writhed on the field for a full minute before the trainer reached him.
The patient had writhed all night before the medication took hold.

senses.head: Squirm from embarrassment
body: Figurative, of acute social discomfort. Often writhe with embarrassment or writhe through something. (ёжиться, корчиться (от стыда, неловкости))
examples: He writhes visibly whenever anyone brings up the old commercial.
She has writhed through worse interviews than that one.
I writhed in my seat for the whole toast.

senses.head: Twist, coil (of a shape)
body: Of snakes, smoke, vines, or roots moving or growing in twisting lines. The archaic writhen meaning "twisted" survives only in poetry; modern prose reaches for twisted or gnarled. (извиваться, скручиваться, виться)
examples: Snakes writhe when you pin them behind the head.
Smoke writhed up from the pile all afternoon.
Old poems describe writhen roots gripping the bare rock.

entries.forms: writhe /raɪð/ · writhed /raɪðd/ · writhen /ˈraɪðən/ · the American participle is writhed /raɪðd/
entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing and description, less common in casual speech
entries.contrast: The w is silent, and the th is the voiced /ð/ of bathe, not the /θ/ of both. Writhen is archaic and poetic; American English uses has writhed, and for a twisted shape it reaches for twisted or gnarled instead. Like rive, the verb now survives mainly in its most physical uses.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and strongly progressive-friendly: he was writhing on the field for a full minute. No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — it never takes an object; the cause follows a preposition: writhe in pain, writhe with embarrassment, writhe through an interview.
entries.passive: no — an intransitive verb has nothing to promote to subject: ✗ the field was writhed on, ✗ worse interviews have been writhed through. The archaic writhen (writhen roots) is an adjective, not a passive participle.
